full.text: The cell membrane
The cell membrane is described by the fluid mosaic model: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins scattered through it.

items: Phospholipids: hydrophilic heads face outwards, hydrophobic tails face inwards
Proteins: channel, carrier, receptor and enzyme proteins
Cholesterol: regulates fluidity in animal cells
Glycoproteins and glycolipids: cell recognition

full.text: Membrane transport
Net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, without using ATP.
Net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane.

Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins but no ATP. Active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient using carrier proteins and ATP. Large particles enter by endocytosis and leave by exocytosis.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: In osmosis questions always use the term water potential, and say water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.

items: Fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer + proteins
Diffusion: high to low concentration, passive
Facilitated diffusion: uses channel/carrier proteins, passive
Osmosis: water, high to low water potential, partially permeable membrane
Active transport: against gradient, needs ATP and carriers
Endocytosis and exocytosis for bulk transport

full.text: The cell cycle
The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S and G2) and the M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis). DNA is replicated in the S phase.
Stages of mitosis

items: Prophase: chromosomes condense, nuclear envelope breaks down, spindle forms
Metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equator, attached to spindle fibres at the centromere
Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
Telophase: nuclear envelopes re-form, chromosomes uncoil

full.text: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm: by a cleavage furrow in animal cells and a cell plate in plant cells.
Nuclear division that produces two genetically identical daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Importance
Mitosis is used for growth, repair of tissues and asexual reproduction.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: Remember PMAT for the order of mitosis, and that anaphase is when chromatids (not homologous chromosomes) separate.

items: Interphase: G1, S (DNA replication), G2
Prophase: condense, envelope breaks, spindle forms
Metaphase: line up at equator
Anaphase: chromatids separate to poles
Telophase: nuclei re-form
Cytokinesis: furrow (animal), cell plate (plant)
Result: 2 identical cells; growth and repair

full.text: Cellular respiration
Respiration releases energy from organic molecules, mainly glucose, and stores it in ATP.
Stages of aerobic respiration

items: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose is split into 2 pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH
Link reaction (mitochondrial matrix): pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA, releasing CO2
Krebs cycle (matrix): acetyl CoA is oxidised, releasing CO2 and producing NADH, FADH2 and ATP
Oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane): the electron transport chain uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor and makes most of the ATP

full.text: Respiration without oxygen; in animals pyruvate forms lactate, in yeast it forms ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Aerobic respiration releases far more ATP per glucose than anaerobic respiration, which only makes the 2 ATP of glycolysis.

full.title: Past-paper tip
full.text: State where each stage happens. Many marks are lost by placing glycolysis in the mitochondrion.

items: Glycolysis: cytoplasm, glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP
Link reaction: pyruvate to acetyl CoA + CO2
Krebs cycle: matrix, CO2, NADH, FADH2
Electron transport chain: inner membrane, O2 final acceptor, most ATP
Anaerobic: lactate (animals), ethanol + CO2 (yeast)

written.stem: Define osmosis and explain what happens to a plant cell placed in a concentrated sugar solution.
written.model_answer: Osmosis is the net movement of water from higher to lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane. In a concentrated solution the outside water potential is lower, so water leaves the cell, the vacuole shrinks and the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).

points.text: Definition: water moves high to low water potential
Plasmolysis / membrane pulls away from wall

written.stem: Describe the events of the four stages of mitosis.
written.model_answer: Prophase: chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down while the spindle forms. Metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear envelopes re-form and chromosomes uncoil.

points.text: Prophase: chromosomes condense / envelope breaks / spindle

written.stem: Explain how temperature affects the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.
written.model_answer: As temperature rises, molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often, so the rate increases up to the optimum temperature. Above the optimum, bonds holding the tertiary structure break, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured, so the rate falls.

points.text: Rate rises with kinetic energy / collisions
Above optimum the active site changes shape

written.stem: Name the stages of aerobic respiration and state where each one takes place.
written.model_answer: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm; the link reaction and Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix; oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

points.text: Oxidative phosphorylation / ETC on the inner membrane

written.stem: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane and explain the ways substances move across it.
written.model_answer: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophobic tails inside and hydrophilic heads outside, with proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins. Small non-polar molecules diffuse through the bilayer; ions and polar molecules use channel or carrier proteins in facilitated diffusion; water moves by osmosis; active transport uses ATP and carriers against the gradient; bulk transport is by endocytosis and exocytosis.

points.text: Phospholipid bilayer with heads and tails

written.stem: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in organisms.
written.model_answer: Both start with glycolysis in the cytoplasm. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, continues through the link reaction, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain in mitochondria and releases much ATP, carbon dioxide and water. Anaerobic respiration has no oxygen; pyruvate becomes lactate in animals or ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast, and only 2 ATP are made per glucose.

points.text: Aerobic yields much ATP, CO2 and water
Anaerobic: ethanol and CO2 in yeast

ask.question: What is osmosis?
ask.answer: Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential through a partially permeable membrane. It is passive and needs no ATP.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 2.8: Cell membrane and membrane transport

ask.question: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
ask.answer: In anaphase the centromeres split and the spindle fibres shorten, pulling the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles of the cell.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 2.9: Cell cycle and mitosis

ask.question: Where does glycolysis take place?
ask.answer: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm. One glucose is split into two pyruvate molecules with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. It does not need oxygen.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 2.14: Cellular respiration

ask.question: How do enzymes work?
ask.answer: An enzyme's active site binds a specific substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex. This lowers the activation energy of the reaction, so it happens faster. The enzyme is not used up.

sources.title: A/L Biology syllabus (2025), topic 2.11: Energy, metabolism and enzymes

ask.question: What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?
ask.answer: Mitosis is one division that gives two genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair. Meiosis is two divisions that give four genetically different haploid cells for sexual reproduction, with crossing over and independent assortment.
